title: 4 days Lower Upper program review (part. 1)
summary: Part one of reviewing a 4-day lower/upper program from his first subscriber, a calisthenics athlete moving to barbell lifts. NH argues bodybuilders can't do short hypertrophy blocks, says pick one king among goals, and fixes the first lower day: one squat style, lower reps for strength work, pause deadlifts over Dimel deadlifts.
claims: Calisthenics is not the best for leg development; pistol squats aren't the same and small legs are an advantage for bodyweight performance
Strength athletes run hypertrophy blocks because they don't otherwise prioritize size; for bodybuilders the whole year is a hypertrophy block
Bodybuilders could instead run occasional strength blocks, but they don't peak performance like powerlifters, so peaking practices don't transfer
You won't see massive hypertrophy in 2-3 months
Chasing calisthenics technique, powerlifting and bodybuilding at once fails; pick one king and make the rest serve it
He does compound movements and calisthenics, but both serve hypertrophy
More tools give more ability to adapt, but you can make do with anything
He usually advises starting the week with an upper day since lower days are high tonnage, and ending on a lower before the weekend rest
With lower days Monday and Thursday, the long gap allows an optional Saturday lower, full body or arm day
Don't trash yourself on lower days; it's injury risk for nothing
Upper/lower is second only to body part splits in freedom
Avoid heavy squats and deadlifts on the same day; if needed, make one heavy and the other moderate or a variation
Once you've found your style, stick to one squat style (high or low bar) and one deadlift style
Constantly rotating styles costs practice and makes it hard to build the program around the main lift; put variations in a week 1/week 2 rotation instead
4x10 is a poor strength-work rep range: too much volume, sandbagged early sets, little progression; use it only for variations
Main squat for 2-4 sets of 4-8 reps, then a secondary knee flexion at 4x10 to fill volume
If you did four heavy squat sets, skip the volume variation since you already got volume
Most people don't know how to box squat; for hypertrophy prefer pause high-bar squats for time under tension and specificity
If squats and deadlifts share a day, squat first: squats load more and pre-fatigued lower back raises risk, while deadlifts can just be dropped
Most people who fail deadlifts at the knee have a setup issue, too rounded, not a strength issue; he used to have that problem
Partial deadlift variations are fine for sticking points but for hypertrophy go deeper with full ROM
Pick conventional or sumo eventually rather than training both
Pause deadlifts off the floor reinforce a tight start and engage abs, lower back, glutes and hamstrings more than Dimel deadlifts
Leg work needs no tons of extensions: heavy knee flexion, maybe a variation, a hip hinge and done
Bulgarian split squats at the end of an already full leg day are greedy; use them as a joker swap
Keep a natural 'joker' lift used about once a month; for him it's good mornings, which trash his hamstrings
3x20 is great for calves; add a set if you like
Hip hinge at 3x5 or 4x4 instead of 4x10; a pause deadlift at 3x5 is heavy but safe
Superset reverse hypers, supermans and calf raises to save time
Early on you don't need a thousand options; a low-exercise program can still be flexible
Strength athletes switching to hypertrophy tend to overdo high reps
Natural bodybuilders don't only do 4x20; strength work must exist year-round for tonnage progression, not just in a block
exercises: better than box squat for hypertrophy
